title: Azide–alkyne cycloaddition
subtitle: Phenyl azide and phenylacetylene give a triazole by a 1,3-dipolar cycloaddition

reactants.caption: phenyl azide + phenylacetylene
reactants.learnerPrompt: The azide's two end nitrogens bond to the two alkyne carbons in one step, making a five-membered ring. Draw the step that gives the 1,4-disubstituted triazole (the two phenyl groups far apart).
hintTiers: Phenyl azide is a 1,3-dipole: three atoms, four π electrons, a negative end and a positive middle. With the two π electrons of an alkyne, that is six electrons moving round a five-membered ring.

The negatively charged end nitrogen bonds to the alkyne carbon carrying the phenyl group; the alkyne CH bonds to the nitrogen carrying phenyl. The N=N π bond between that nitrogen and the middle nitrogen becomes a lone pair on the middle nitrogen. Three arrows.

Arrow 1: lone pair on the end (negative) nitrogen to a new bond to the phenyl-bearing alkyne carbon. Arrow 2: from one alkyne π bond to a new bond between the alkyne CH and the phenyl-bearing nitrogen. Arrow 3: from the π bond between that nitrogen and the middle nitrogen to a lone pair on the middle nitrogen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: The middle nitrogen of the azide makes no new bond. The two end nitrogens bond to the two alkyne carbons, closing a five-membered ring.
Losing N₂ to make a nitrene needs much harsher heating or light. With an alkyne present, the whole azide adds and all three nitrogens end up in the ring.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right start. The alkyne CH must now bond to the other end of the azide, and the electrons on that end move inwards. Two more arrows.

triazole-1-5.caption: 1,5-diphenyl-1H-1,2,3-triazole, the other regioisomer, also formed on heating

steps.explanationAfterStep: A [3+2] cycloaddition: four electrons from the azide and two from the alkyne move round a five-membered ring in one step, and the product is an aromatic 1,2,3-triazole. Thermally, the two orientations have similar frontier-orbital matches, so heating gives both the 1,4- and the 1,5-isomer in comparable amounts. With copper(I) catalysis (the “click” reaction, not drawn here: copper is not in the app yet) only the 1,4-isomer forms, at room temperature.
Correct arrows for the other orientation: the 1,5-isomer, with the phenyl groups side by side. On heating this forms alongside the 1,4-isomer; the copper-catalysed version avoids it.

mechanismSummary: Organic azides are 1,3-dipoles: three atoms sharing four π electrons. They add across alkynes in a concerted [3+2] cycloaddition (Huisgen), a six-electron pericyclic reaction like the Diels–Alder, to give aromatic 1,2,3-triazoles. A terminal alkyne can add either way round, and on heating both regioisomers form. Copper(I) catalysis (CuAAC, “click” chemistry) goes by a different, stepwise mechanism and gives only the 1,4-isomer.
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 34
